issues.item: Triggers: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: The trigger 'being in a situation where someone has power over me' is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type of natural disaster and with the rest of the profile, which otherwise emphasizes alarm/reactivity and fragmented recall rather than interpersonal domination or coercion. For this trauma type, this item introduces an implausible trigger theme not supported elsewhere in threat, memory, or appraisals.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Avoiding hospitals/ambulances/physical examinations is not well supported by the rest of the profile for a natural-disaster trauma. There are no memory or threat items involving injury treatment, medical rescue, or bodily harm, so this strategy appears to target a symptom theme not represented elsewhere. In contrast, the profile is centered on generalized alarm, shouting, unpredictability, and fragmented memory.

issues.item: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
issues.explanation: Self-harm is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma context: the other selected items describe a classic hyperarousal/re-experiencing natural-disaster PTSD presentation with avoidance and overeating, but no accompanying items suggest the kind of shame, self-punitive appraisal, dissociative affect regulation, or broader emotion-dysregulation pattern that would make physical self-harm clinically coherent here. It stands out as addressing a symptom process not otherwise represented in the five components.

Alcohol smell is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly anchored to the reported trauma type and the rest of the item set. The other triggers (unpredictability, shouting) fit a danger/hyperarousal formulation, whereas alcohol smell implies a very specific sensory trauma cue that is not supported by the memory or threat items. Given a natural-disaster index trauma, this trigger is difficult to explain clinically without additional corroborating content.

vignette: John, a 55-year-old African-American married man who works as a Bomb Disposal Technician, has been struggling with symptoms of PTSD since he experienced a devastating natural disaster several months ago. John's life changed dramatically when an unexpected and powerful tornado hit his city, destroying buildings, causing chaos, and leaving a trail of destruction in its wake. John vividly remembers the day the tornado struck. He was on duty, having just finished disarming a complex device at a construction site. As he prepared to leave, the sky darkened suddenly, and the wind picked up with an intensity he had never felt before. Within minutes, debris began flying through the air, and John found himself trapped amidst collapsing structures. The unpredictability of the disaster left him feeling helpless and exposed, his body reacting as if he were in immediate danger even when there was no clear threat. Since that day, John has been hyper-vigilant and prone to false alarms. Small triggers like unpredictable situations, loud noises, or sudden shouting set off intense reactions. His heightened state of arousal often leads him to react as though he is in imminent danger, even when his environment is safe. For instance, the sound of a fire alarm going off at work can instantly transport John back to that day, where he feels the panic and fear all over again. John has developed several maladaptive strategies to cope with his distress. He often turns to food as an escape, eating excessively to manage the overwhelming emotions. His diet has become unhealthier over time, leading to weight gain and a general decline in physical health. Additionally, John tries to avoid anything that could be stressful, even if it means avoiding social gatherings or skipping family events. This constant avoidance of stressors has strained his relationship with his wife, who feels increasingly isolated. John is also prone to keeping his mind occupied all the time as a form of mental distraction. He finds himself constantly thinking about work or any other activity that can keep him busy, leaving little room for relaxation or reflection. At times, he even skips meals to stay focused on tasks, which further exacerbates his physical health issues. When John does recall the traumatic event, it is often fragmented and incomplete. Memories of the tornado come in pieces, with gaps that make it difficult for him to form a coherent picture of what happened. What frightens him most about these memories is not just their intensity but also the intense rage they evoke. He feels like his body reacts before he has time to think, leading to moments where he lashes out at small irritations or perceived threats. John's job as a Bomb Disposal Technician exacerbates his symptoms. The unpredictability of his work environment and the constant presence of loud noises serve as potent triggers for his PTSD symptoms. He often finds himself on high alert while on duty, which affects his performance and decision-making abilities. John has started avoiding certain assignments that he believes could be too stressful or dangerous, leading to conflicts with his supervisors who expect him to fulfill all his duties. John's world has become a web of avoidance and hypervigilance, making everyday life increasingly difficult. He had come to believe that only by constantly monitoring his environment could he prevent another traumatic event from happening again. However, this constant state of alertness leaves him feeling exhausted and anxious. What finally brought John to seek help was the realization that his symptoms were not only affecting his work but also straining his relationship with his wife. He is most afraid that if he doesn't get better, he will lose her completely. At the same time, he hopes for a future where he can live without being constantly on edge and where he can regain control over his life. John's current state reflects a desperate need to reclaim some sense of normalcy and control. He is eager to work with a therapist who understands the complexities of his trauma and can help him navigate through his fears and memories. His journey toward healing will involve learning how to manage his triggers, process his memories, and regain confidence in his ability to cope with life's unpredictabilities.
